nature-hist-007.title: Climate change: a warming world and why it matters
nature-hist-007.text: 2024 was the warmest year on record, at +1.60 °C since regular tracking began in 1850. Present-day climate change is global warming, the ongoing rise in Earth's average temperature, together with its wider effects on the climate system. Human activity drives it. The chief cause is burning coal, oil and gas since the Industrial Revolution, joined by deforestation and some farming and industrial practices that release heat-trapping gases. The atmosphere now holds roughly 50% more carbon dioxide than at the end of the pre-industrial era. The consequences include more flooding, extreme heat, food and water shortages, disease and economic loss. The burden falls unevenly: the poorest communities, who emitted least, are the most vulnerable. Under the 2015 {{ref:nature-clim-074}}, nations agreed to keep warming well under 2 °C, yet current pledges would still lead to about 2.8 °C by 2100. Warming can be limited by cutting emissions and by removing carbon dioxide from the air. As of 2019, {{ref:nature-pol-239}} covered about 20% of global emissions. The science is old. Joseph Fourier proposed in the 1820s that the air traps heat, the idea explained in {{ref:nature-eco-161}}. Climate change reached international public attention in the late 1980s.

nature-eco-161.title: The greenhouse effect: Earth's heat-trapping blanket
nature-eco-161.text: Without the greenhouse effect, Earth's surface would average −18 °C. With it, the average is about 15 °C. The greenhouse effect is the warming of a planet's surface that happens when heat-trapping gases in its atmosphere stop it losing heat to space. It works in two steps. Sunlight passes through these gases and heats Earth's surface. The warm surface then gives off longwave heat radiation, which the gases mostly absorb. Adding more of these gases through human activity strengthens the effect, which is called the enhanced greenhouse effect. That extra heat-trapping has been observed directly, and it is mainly due to more carbon dioxide in the air. The idea is nearly two centuries old. Joseph Fourier proposed the effect as early as 1824, and in 1856 Eunice Newton Foote showed that carbon dioxide strengthens the sun's warming of air. The name is a little misleading, though. Real greenhouses keep heat mainly by blocking moving air, not by absorbing radiation.

nature-eco-162.title: Greenhouse gases: the trace gases that warm the world
nature-eco-162.text: Nitrogen and oxygen make up 99% of dry air, yet they barely absorb heat radiation. Carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide, under 0.1% of the air, do. A greenhouse gas is a gas in an atmosphere that traps heat and so raises the surface temperature of a planet such as Earth. It absorbs the heat radiation the planet gives off, and that produces the greenhouse effect. Water vapour causes 41–67% of the effect, but human activity does not directly change its global level. Most of the carbon dioxide people add comes from burning fossil fuels, plus cement, fertilizer and land-use change such as deforestation. Emissions reached an all-time high of 53.6±5.2 Gt CO2e per year over 2014–2023. That unit counts every gas by the amount of carbon dioxide that would warm as much, as {{ref:nature-eco-160}} explains. In 2022 the IPCC warned that emissions must peak before 2025 and fall 43% by 2030 for a good chance of limiting warming to 1.5 °C.

nature-eco-163.title: Greenhouse gas emissions: who emits, and how much
nature-eco-163.text: Global emissions run at about 50 Gt a year, and the estimate for 2024 was 57.7 Gt CO2eq. Greenhouse gas emissions are releases of greenhouse gases from human activities, which strengthen the greenhouse effect and drive climate change. Carbon dioxide from burning coal, oil and natural gas is the main cause. By sector, the power sector contributes about 27%, transport 15%, and industrial energy and agriculture 11% each. Emissions began rising with fossil-fuelled industry around 1750 and grew rapidly after about 1950. China emits the most each year, followed by the United States, which emits more per person. Average emissions of 4.9 tonnes per person a year are over twice the 2.3 tonnes consistent with the 1.5 °C goal. There is one hopeful sign: 2015 was the first year with both global economic growth and falling carbon emissions.

nature-eco-007.title: Carbon dioxide: the gas at the center of the story
nature-eco-007.text: In 2026 the air held 432 ppm of carbon dioxide, or 0.0432%. That is a 54% rise from the 280 ppm of the 10,000 years before the mid-18th century. Carbon dioxide is a trace gas in Earth's air, yet it plays a central part in the greenhouse effect, the carbon cycle and photosynthesis. It is one of the three principal greenhouse gases in Earth's atmosphere, and today's concentration is the highest for 14 million years. The rise is caused by human activity, mainly burning fossil fuels, with cement making, deforestation and biomass burning adding more. Human emissions exceed what natural sinks can absorb, so about half of the carbon dioxide from fossil fuels stays in the air. By 2024 humans had emitted an estimated 2,650 gigatonnes since 1850, at 42 gigatonnes a year, and about 1,050 gigatonnes remain in the air. A projected 20–35% of the fossil carbon released so far will keep levels raised for many thousands of years. The rise is tracked at Mauna Loa, where regular measurements began in 1958, building on Dave Keeling's accurate flask samples of the 1950s.

nature-eco-011.title: Observed warming: what the thermometers show
nature-eco-011.text: The decade from 2016 to 2025 averaged 1.26 °C above the 1850–1900 baseline, and 2024 alone was more than 1.5 °C above it. Observed global warming is this rise in Earth's average surface temperature, measured since thermometer records reached global coverage around 1850. Datasets agree that surface temperature is rising by around 0.2 °C per decade. Scientists measure warming as a 20-year average, because natural variability can make a single year 0.2 °C warmer or colder. The path was not smooth. Up to 1970 there was little net warming, because sulfur dioxide pollution reflected sunlight and offset greenhouse warming. After that, warming sped up. Most of the extra heat is out of sight: over 90% of it since 1970 has gone into the ocean. Land has warmed almost twice as fast as the global average, and the Arctic three to four times faster than the rest of the world. Other signs include retreating glaciers, heavier rain, earlier spring flowering and thousands of species moving to cooler areas.

nature-eco-017.title: The effects of climate change, from reefs to economies
nature-eco-017.text: Damage climbs steeply with temperature: one comparison found total damages at 1.5 °C were 90% lower than at 3.66 °C. The effects of climate change are its well-documented and growing impacts on the natural world and on human societies. They include a warming trend, shifting rainfall and more weather extremes, with fiercer fires, thawing permafrost and spreading deserts. Some changes can become irreversible once tipping points are crossed. Oceans and ice sheets absorb most of the extra heat. That delays some effects, which then continue after surface temperatures settle, and makes {{ref:nature-clim-037}} a major long-term concern. Mountains, coral reefs and the Arctic are the most immediately threatened ecosystems. At 2 °C, about 10% of land species would become critically endangered. For people, food and water supplies, health, farming, fisheries and forestry are at risk, and heat stress will limit outdoor work in the tropics. The burden is unequal. Poor people, children and Indigenous peoples are especially at risk, while rich industrialised countries, which emitted most carbon dioxide, have more resources to adapt. Wealthy colder countries have felt little economic harm or even gained, while poor hot countries probably grew less than they would have.

nature-eco-001.title: Extreme weather: the far ends of the range
nature-eco-001.text: Since the 1920s, death tolls from natural disasters have fallen over 90 percent, even as population quadrupled. Extreme weather is unexpected, unusual, severe or unseasonal weather at the far ends of the range a place has seen in the past. The main types are heat waves, cold waves, droughts, and heavy rain or storms such as tropical cyclones. The IPCC counts an event as extreme if it is as rare as or rarer than the 10th or 90th percentile of observed weather. Severe weather, which threatens life and property, is one kind. Natural variability, such as El Niño, explains some extremes, but system-wide changes can raise their frequency or intensity. Warmer air holds more moisture, so storms can drop more rain and cause floods and landslides. Paving land and destroying wetlands, which store water naturally, can make floods worse. The toll on food is measurable: drought and extreme heat cut national cereal production by 10% over 1964–2007.

nature-eco-004.title: Radiative forcing: the push on Earth's energy balance
nature-eco-004.text: Radiative forcing is a measure of how much a change, such as more greenhouse gas, shifts the balance of energy flowing into and out of the atmosphere. It is measured in watts per square meter, usually averaged over the whole globe. A planet in radiative equilibrium, with as much energy leaving as arriving, has zero net forcing and a steady temperature. Greenhouse gases, aerosols, which are tiny particles in the air, surface reflectivity and the sun's output all change Earth's energy balance. The IPCC puts human-caused forcing in 2019 at 2.72 W/m2 relative to 1750, within a range of 1.96 to 3.48. Most comes from greenhouse gases, partly offset by aerosols. The 50% rise in carbon dioxide since 1750, as of 2020, corresponds to +2.17 W/m2. Its effect weakens as it accumulates. The forcing is roughly ΔF = 5.35 × ln((C0+ΔC)/C0) W/m2, so each further increase warms less.

nature-eco-159.title: Global warming potential: comparing gases with carbon dioxide
nature-eco-159.text: Over 20 years, methane traps 81.2 times as much heat as the same mass of carbon dioxide; over 100 years, only 27.9 times. Global warming potential, or GWP, measures how much heat a greenhouse gas traps over a set period compared with the same mass of carbon dioxide. By definition carbon dioxide has a GWP of 1. A gas's GWP depends on how strongly it absorbs heat radiation, how fast it leaves the air, and the time frame chosen. Methane's two figures differ because it leaves the atmosphere much faster than carbon dioxide. Regulators usually use a 100-year time scale, and international agreements have adopted it as the standard. Since 1997, reporting under the {{ref:nature-clim-056}} has used fixed IPCC values to convert gases into the common unit described in {{ref:nature-eco-160}}. Other metrics include the global temperature change potential and GWP*, which treats short-lived pollutants such as methane differently.

nature-eco-014.title: Climate feedbacks: how warming amplifies or tames itself
nature-eco-014.text: Climate change feedbacks are processes set off by an initial warming that either amplify it, called positive feedbacks, or dampen it, called negative feedbacks. The main amplifiers are water vapour, melting ice, which leaves a darker surface behind, and the net effect of clouds. The main balancing mechanism is simple: a warmer surface gives off more heat to space. The Arctic shows the amplifiers at work. Shrinking snow and sea ice make the surface darker, speeding Arctic warming and helping thaw permafrost, which releases methane and carbon dioxide. Carbon sinks respond too. Land and oceans have absorbed about half of human carbon dioxide. That share could rise to about 70% if emissions fall, but drop below 40% if they rise sharply. Feedbacks are expected to become more positive as emissions continue, raising the {{ref:nature-eco-158}}. Uncertainty about feedbacks, especially clouds, is the main reason computer models of the climate disagree on how much warming a given amount of emissions causes.

nature-eco-009.title: The main greenhouse gases and how long they linger
nature-eco-009.text: Water vapour causes about 50% of Earth's natural greenhouse effect and clouds about 25%, yet neither counts as a driver of climate change. The main greenhouse gases are the ones that do most of the heat-trapping in Earth's atmosphere: water vapour, carbon dioxide, ozone, methane and nitrous oxide, plus clouds. Without this natural effect, Earth's surface would average about −18 °C instead of around 15 °C. Water vapour and clouds change with temperature, so scientists treat them as feedbacks. Carbon dioxide, which causes about 20% of the effect, changes independently of temperature. So do ozone in the lower atmosphere, the industrial chemicals called CFCs, and nitrous oxide. These count as external forcings. Human emissions in 2019 equalled 59 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide: 75% was carbon dioxide, 18% methane, 4% nitrous oxide and 2% fluorinated gases. Methane comes from livestock, wetlands, rice, landfills, coal mining and oil and gas. Nitrous oxide comes mostly from microbes breaking down fertilizer. Lifetimes differ widely. Methane lasts about 12 years in the air on average, while carbon dioxide lasts much longer. In the IPCC table, nitrous oxide lasts 121 years with a 100-year GWP of 265, and some fluorinated gases are far stronger, such as SF6 at 23,500. By 2022, carbon dioxide had risen about 50% and methane 164% since 1750.

nature-eco-013.title: Fingerprints: how scientists pin warming on people
nature-eco-013.text: The sun is not to blame. Its energy reaching Earth has shown no upward trend since 1880, and the upper atmosphere is cooling rather than warming. Scientists identify the causes of recent warming by comparing the fingerprints of each possible cause with observed patterns. Natural cycles such as El Niño cause short-term spikes and dips. Longer changes come from external forcings: greenhouse gases, the sun, volcanoes and Earth's orbit. Volcanic carbon dioxide equals less than 1% of human emissions, and natural forcings have had negligible effect on temperature trends since the Industrial Revolution. That leaves human activity, mainly burning coal, oil and gas, which has raised greenhouse gas levels. Some human effects cool. Aerosols from air pollution have a smaller cooling effect, and changes in land use have so far slightly cooled the planet by making surfaces more reflective. Natural sinks absorb part of each year's emissions: land removes about 29%, and the ocean absorbed 20 to 30% over the last two decades.

nature-eco-015.title: Climate models: simulating the planet
nature-eco-015.text: A climate model represents the physical, chemical and biological processes that shape the climate system, and it is used to project future warming. Models are tested by checking how well they reproduce present and past climates. They are not perfect: past models underestimated how fast Arctic ice would shrink and rainfall would increase. Some models add population, economic growth and energy use to produce emission scenarios, which feed physical and carbon cycle models. Depending on the scenario, they give carbon dioxide concentrations from 380 to 1400 ppm.

nature-eco-158.title: Climate sensitivity: the warming from doubled carbon dioxide
nature-eco-158.text: Double the carbon dioxide in the air, and how much hotter does Earth get? Climate sensitivity is the answer. Doubling carbon dioxide gives a forcing of about 3.7 W/m2, which without feedbacks would cause roughly 1 °C of warming. But warming triggers feedbacks, such as melting ice and more water vapour, whose strength is not known exactly. In 1990 the IPCC put equilibrium sensitivity between 1.5 and 4.5 °C. Observations and physics now give a very likely range of 2.3 to 4.7 °C. The number carries a large price tag. The cost of cutting emissions depends on how fast carbon neutrality is needed, so sensitivity has large economic and policy consequences. One study suggests that halving the uncertainty in the transient climate response, a shorter-term version of the measure, could save trillions of dollars. If sensitivity is high, the Paris goal of well below 2 °C cannot be met, at least temporarily.

nature-eco-012.title: Projected warming: what the coming decades may bring
nature-eco-012.text: The IPCC expects the 20-year average to pass +1.5 °C in the early 2030s. Projected future warming is the estimate of how much hotter Earth will get, and it depends mainly on future greenhouse gas emissions. By 2100 warming is very likely to reach 1.0–1.8 °C with very low emissions, 2.1–3.5 °C with intermediate emissions, or 3.3–5.7 °C with very high emissions. In the intermediate and high scenarios, warming continues past 2100. The remaining carbon dioxide that can still be emitted for a given temperature limit, the {{ref:nature-clim-136}}, comes from modelling the carbon cycle and climate sensitivity. UNEP says a 50% chance of staying below 2.0 °C allows 900 gigatonnes of carbon dioxide after 2023. That is about 16 years of current emissions.

nature-eco-160.title: Carbon dioxide equivalent: one scale for many gases
nature-eco-160.text: Two tonnes of a gas with a global warming potential of 100 count as 200 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent, or CO2e. That is the arithmetic of the unit: the mass of carbon dioxide that would warm the Earth as much as a given mass of another greenhouse gas. It gives one common scale for the climate effects of different gases. It is calculated as the gas's global warming potential times its mass. Values depend on the time scale chosen, usually 100 or 20 years. The unit matters for money, because carbon markets and {{ref:nature-pol-081}} schemes price emissions per tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent.

nature-eco-002.title: What extreme weather costs economies
nature-eco-002.text: A 2023 study put the cost of climate-driven extreme weather at about US$2.86 trillion over 2000–2019, roughly US$143 billion a year. The economic cost of extreme weather is the monetary loss such events cause to economies. In 2011 the IPCC estimated that annual losses since 1980 ranged from a few billion to above US$200 billion, peaking in 2005, the year of Hurricane Katrina. These figures understate the harm. Losses of lives, cultural heritage and ecosystem services are hard to put a price on, so loss estimates reflect them poorly. The risk is widely felt: in the 2023–2024 World Economic Forum risk survey, 66 percent of respondents named extreme weather a top risk.

nature-eco-010.title: Water vapour feedback: warming that breeds more warming
nature-eco-010.text: Water vapour causes 41–67% of the greenhouse effect, yet people do not directly change its global level. It stays in the air only about nine days, so local changes such as irrigation have little global effect. Temperature controls it instead. A law of physics, the Clausius–Clapeyron relation, means warmer air holds more water vapour per unit volume. That creates the water vapour feedback: warming lets the air hold more water vapour, a greenhouse gas, which adds further warming.

nature-eco-019.title: Climate change and the world's food supply
nature-eco-019.text: Disasters from extreme weather caused food production losses estimated at US$123 billion in 2025, 5% of global agricultural GDP. Climate change threatens people's ability to grow, reach and rely on enough food. The causes include higher carbon dioxide, heat, changed rainfall, more extreme events, and shifting pests and diseases. Climate change is projected to weaken the food supply on every front, affecting how much food exists, its price and quality, and how stable the supply is. The sea is affected too. Ocean biomass is expected to fall by about 5% per degree of warming, hitting tropical seas hardest.

nature-eco-020.title: The economic sectors most exposed to climate
nature-eco-020.text: Climate-sensitive sectors are the parts of the economy most exposed to climate change, because they depend directly on weather: farming, fishing, forestry, tourism and energy. Thermal power plants need cooling water and run less efficiently when hot, while hydropower suffers when river flows fall. Heat, lower water flow and changed rainfall could cut total energy production by 7% a year by the end of the century. Insurance premiums are rising, and Munich Re warned in 2019 that home insurance could become unaffordable for average-income households. Above 1.5 °C of warming, tourism and outdoor work may reach the limits of how far they can adapt.

nature-eco-018.title: How climate change harms human health
nature-eco-018.text: Climate change harms health in many ways, from heat illness and worse air to disease spread and extreme weather. Longer exposure to high temperatures can cause heat illness and heat-related deaths. Diseases spread by mosquitoes and ticks, such as dengue fever and malaria, may become more common in some regions, as may waterborne diseases. Lower crop yields can raise food prices and cause undernutrition, and clean water supplies can shrink. Together these can increase poverty, migration, violent conflict and mental health problems.

nature-eco-021.title: Melting ice sheets and the long rise of the seas
nature-eco-021.text: Losing the whole West Antarctic ice sheet would raise sea level by over 5 metres. Ice sheet decline is the melting of the Greenland and West Antarctic ice sheets, which will keep raising sea levels over long time-scales. A partial collapse in West Antarctica could be abrupt and irreversible for centuries or longer. Sustained warming between 1 °C and 4 °C would melt the Greenland ice sheet entirely over millennia, adding 7 m to sea levels. The melting feeds itself. As the ice surface melts it gets lower and warmer, a self-reinforcing feedback that can make the loss irreversible.

nature-eco-008.title: CO2 fertilization: more carbon, faster photosynthesis
nature-eco-008.text: Earth's land has greened markedly since the early 1980s. Part of the reason is the CO2 fertilization effect: the speeding-up of plant photosynthesis, with less water lost through leaves, caused by more carbon dioxide in the air. It has been reported to cause 44% of the increase in gross primary productivity since the 2000s. Its strength depends on plant species, temperature and the water and nutrients available. But faster photosynthesis does not always mean more growth or carbon storage, and plants are unlikely to cut carbon dioxide levels much over the next century.

nature-eco-003.title: Extreme event attribution: weighing climate's role
nature-eco-003.text: Was that heat wave caused by climate change? A single extreme event generally cannot be blamed on any one cause. Extreme event attribution instead works out how far causes such as climate change explain trends in extreme weather events. Much of the work relies on climate models, which are vital but only approximations.

nature-eco-005.title: The climate sensitivity parameter: turning forcing into degrees
nature-eco-005.text: The climate sensitivity parameter is a number, in kelvin per W/m2, that links a radiative forcing to the eventual change in surface temperature. A kelvin is the same size as a degree Celsius. The parameter is the inverse of the climate feedback parameter. A value of about 0.8 gives about 1.6 K of warming since 1750 from carbon dioxide rising from 278 to 405 ppm, a forcing of 2.0 W/m2. The same value predicts a further 1.4 K of warming if carbon dioxide doubled from its pre-industrial level.

nature-eco-006.title: Earth's albedo: the share of sunlight bounced back
nature-eco-006.text: Earth reflects about 30% of incoming sunlight back to space, giving Earth's albedo a value of 0.30 on annual average. Clouds, aerosols, oceans, land, snow, ice and vegetation do the reflecting, and Earth absorbs the other 70%. Human changes push both ways. Deforestation typically raises reflectivity, while Arctic ice loss lowers it.

nature-eco-016.title: Earth system sensitivity: warming over millennia
nature-eco-016.text: Earth system sensitivity measures the long-term warming from doubled carbon dioxide, including slow feedbacks, such as melting ice sheets and changing vegetation, that take millennia. These slower feedbacks make it larger than equilibrium climate sensitivity, possibly twice as large. It is estimated from Earth's geological history, so future values are highly uncertain.

openers.climate-science-essentials: Without the gases that trap heat in its air, Earth's surface would average −18 °C instead of about 15 °C. This chapter explains that greenhouse effect, the gases behind it, and how human emissions of those gases, above all carbon dioxide, are strengthening it. It follows the rise in average temperature measured since thermometer records reached global coverage around 1850, along with the extreme weather and wider effects that come with it. Along the way it introduces the yardsticks scientists use to compare causes: radiative forcing, global warming potential, and the feedbacks that amplify or dampen an initial warming.

reviews.climate-science-essentials: Sunlight warms Earth's surface, and greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide hold in part of the heat it gives off. Burning coal, oil and gas has raised carbon dioxide by roughly half, strengthening that effect, and thermometers show the result as a rise of around 0.2 °C per decade. Scientists compare causes with tools such as radiative forcing, global warming potential and carbon dioxide equivalent, and they weigh how feedbacks and climate sensitivity amplify the push. The effects reach from melting ice sheets and extreme weather to farming, fisheries, energy, health and the wider economy, and they fall hardest on the poorest people, who emitted least.
